newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico polls show ruling party heading for defeat.
newsitem.headline: Mexico polls show ruling party heading for defeat.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo's party is heading for its worst result ever in congressional elections on July 6, according to the last opinion polls published before a ban on surveys takes effect Saturday.

Four national surveys published on Thursday and Friday showed Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) losing its 68-year-old grip on the lower house of congress, though they differed over the margin of the setback.

More bad news for Zedillo came from polls in the capital city, which all pointed to a huge victory in the mayor's election for a man many see as the PRI's nemesis, veteran left-winger Cuauhtemoc Cardenas.

Many Mexicans believe Cardenas was the real winner of the 1988 presidential election, which officially went to the PRI's Carlos Salinas amid allegations of massive fraud. The PRI always denied wrongdoing but ordered the voting papers to be burned to prevent a recount.

On July 6, Mexicans will elect a new Chamber of Deputies, a quarter of the Senate, six state governors and, for the first time, a mayor of Mexico City. Previous mayors of the capital were always nominated by the president.
The PRI's huge Senate majority is not threatened by the renewal of just a quarter of senators.

But the loss of its lower house majority could cause big headaches for Zedillo in getting reforms and the annual budget passed. The Mexican constitution gives the lower house exclusive responsibility for the annual budget and accounts.

Such is the concern that Reforma reported on Friday that PRI deputies were considering calling an emergency session of congress to pass an early 1998 budget and forestall any problems from a possible opposition majority in the lower house. There was no immediate official comment on the report.

Mexico's president has traditionally enjoyed enormous power because the PRI majority in congress unfailingly rubber-stamped all his legislation. The PRI had 302 of the 500 seats in the outgoing Chamber of Deputies.

An opposition majority in Congress would send an earthquake through the Mexican political system and could mark the beginning of the end of the PRI's 68-year domination of the country, political analysts say.

Reforma's national poll and a similar survey by the Guadalajara University's Centre for Opinion Studies (CEO), both of whom have a relatively good track record in past elections, showed a big reverse for the PRI in the congressional vote.
Reforma predicted the PRI would win just 36.7 percent of the vote, against 55.6 percent for the two biggest opposition parties combined, based on projections that excluded don't knows.

This is way down on the 50.2 percent of the vote the PRI won in the last congressional elections held in August 1994, just four months before a disastrous peso devaluation that plunged the country into recession.

CEO saw the PRI crashing to just 30.7 percent of the vote, practically level with its biggest challenger, the conservative National Action Party (PAN) with 30.0 percent. The left-wing PRD followed with 20.9 percent.
CEO's figures did not exclude 13.6 percent of respondents who did not know which way they would vote or did not reply.

Two other polls, from the Covarrubias and Consulta organisations who other pollsters say have worked for the PRI, put the ruling party further ahead of the opposition, but still just short of the level it needs for a lower house majority.

Senior government sources confirmed to Reuters that President Zedillo had been holding top-level talks with members of his inner circle during the past few weeks to discuss how he might cope with an opposition majority in congress.

"It's clear that whatever the result is, we are going to have to dedicate much more time to lobbying in Congress," one official said. "There may well be changes in the way the government is organised to take account of this."
